edits.before: Spatial tuning gives a second example. In the hippocampus, a brain structure involved in memory and navigation, a [**place cell**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} fires strongly in one or more localized regions of an environment. A connected region of elevated spatial firing is a [**place field**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. One neuron can have several fields. A [**rate map**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} estimates the rate at each position by dividing the spikes recorded there by the time spent there. Sparse visits, smoothing, and firing cutoffs therefore affect the estimated map and its fields. A field in a model's expected rate and a field extracted from finite recordings are related objects with different measurement uncertainties.[^f-place]

edits.before: The [**Brownian motion**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} $W(t)$ starts at zero, has independent Gaussian increments, and satisfies $\operatorname{Var}[W(t)-W(s)]=t-s$ for $t\geq s$. It describes the limit of many small, suitably independent fluctuations. A physical network need only approach this description over the time and noise scales relevant to the calculation. The parameter $D$ is its [**diffusion coefficient**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. It measures the rate of variance growth; a single trajectory need not move monotonically away from its starting value.

edits.before: The [**mean squared displacement**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, or MSD, is the expected squared change across a lag. In the zero-mean diffusion just defined, MSD is $2Dt$. A [**root mean squared displacement**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is its square root, $\sqrt{2Dt}$, and has the same units as the represented coordinate. In several dimensions, adding independent coordinate contributions gives an overall MSD of $2dDt$ only when each of the $d$ coordinates has the same diffusion coefficient. A paper that defines its diffusion parameter as the entire two-dimensional MSD slope uses a different convention.

edits.before: Looking steadily at a small spot does not hold the eye perfectly still. Between brief, rapid movements called [**microsaccades**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, the eye makes a small, smooth, irregular movement called [**fixational drift**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. Does this movement begin as noise in the muscles, or does the brain send a changing command to them? Ben-Shushan and colleagues answer this in two stages. Their recordings support a large shared drive upstream of the motor neurons. Their model then proposes a particular source: random motion of the eye position stored in a memory circuit.[^p2-question]
